content: Occlusion in dentistry refers to the contact between the upper (maxillary) and lower (mandibular) teeth. More specifically, it describes the relationship between these teeth when they come together, such as during chewing or when the jaw is at rest. Malocclusion, or a bad bite, occurs when there is misalignment of the teeth or jaws. This condition can lead to various dental and health issues. Static occlusion refers to the contact between teeth when the jaw is closed and not moving. In contrast, dynamic occlusion describes the contact between teeth when the jaw is in motion, such as during chewing. Centric occlusion is the position where a person’s teeth come together in maximum intercuspation when the jaw is closed. This is often referred to as the habitual bite, bite of convenience, or intercuspation position (ICP). Centric relation, however, is a distinct concept that describes the positional relationship between the upper and lower jaws, independent of tooth contact. Malocclusion can result in a variety of complications, not only affecting the teeth but also the gums, temporomandibular joint (TMJ), and jaw muscles. Teeth, as well as dental restorations like fillings and crowns, may wear down, fracture, or become loose. Additionally, teeth may become tender or painful. A misaligned bite can worsen gum recession. TMJ disorders, collectively referred to as temporomandibular joint disorder or TMJ syndrome, may manifest as clicking, grinding, or pain in the jaw joint, as well as symptoms like tinnitus (ringing or buzzing in the ears) and difficulty opening or closing the mouth. When the jaw is misaligned, the muscles of the jaw may need to exert extra effort, potentially leading to muscle fatigue or spasms. This can result in secondary symptoms such as headaches or migraines, pain around the eyes or sinuses, and discomfort in the neck, shoulders, or even the back. If left untreated, severe malocclusion can cause occlusal trauma, which may further damage the teeth and surrounding structures. Treatment options for occlusal problems vary depending on the severity and underlying cause. These may include tooth adjustments, replacement of missing teeth, temporary use of medications, dietary modifications to include softer foods, and relaxation therapy to address stress-related clenching or grinding. Orthodontic appliances, such as fixed braces, can be used to correct occlusion, while removable devices like occlusal splints may serve both corrective and protective purposes.
